newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Amnesty says bring Khmer Rouge to justice.
newsitem.headline: Amnesty says bring Khmer Rouge to justice.

text.p: Cambodia's notorious Khmer Rouge guerrillas, whose defence chief was said to have been killed along with his family by the movement's leader Pol Pot this week, must be brought to justice, Amnesty International said.

"The world remembers with horror the gross human rights violations committed during the 1975-1979 Khmer Rouge government, as well as continuing abuses of human rights after their fall from power," the international human rights group said in a statement released on Saturday.
"It is time to hold individuals accountable for their actions, and to bring to justice those against whom there is credible evidence."
London-based Amnesty said senior Khmer Rouge officials could be charged with crimes against humanity.

Cambodian co-Premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh on Friday said Pol Pot, mastermind of Cambodia's "killing fields" reign of terror, had killed his defence chief, Son Sen, and 11 of his family members and fled his northern stronghold.
He shot them dead and ran them over with a truck, he said.
Ranariddh, who said he had photographic evidence of the killings, told reporters the ailing Pol Pot was carried off by his men in a sling.
A senior Cambodian military official said on Saturday Pol Pot was in the jungle east of his northern stronghold of Anlong Veng. No other details were immediately available.
Amnesty said the internal strife in the Khmer Rouge represented a rare opportunity for the Cambodian government to bring the rebels to justice.
"If this opportunity is lost, Cambodians may never again have the chance to establish the truth about their recent past...," the statement said.
Ranariddh has said he supports bringing Pol Pot to justice but has expressed willingness to forgive other leaders, including Khmer Rouge front man and nominal leader, Khieu Samphan.
Ranariddh's father, King Norodom Sihanouk, and co-Premier Hun Sen, have both said they want an internatonal tribunal to try the guerrilla leaders.
The Khmer Rouge are held responsible for the deaths of more than a million Cambodians from 1975-1979 through murder, torture, starvation or disease.
The rebels reneged on a 1991 peace pact and have been fighting the coalition government formed following U.N.-sponsored polls in 1993.
But the organisation has been decimated by thousands of defections to government forces since last August, and fewer than 2,000 hard-liners are thought to be still fighting.
